SOLACE

Volume Three — Act II: The City Learns His Name

Chaotic Designs

"The light stays on."

PAGE 1 — THE CITY LEARNS HIS NAME

Panel 1.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the café's back room at night — Rae Mercer at the radio desk, headset on, a wall map behind her that was bare a month ago and is not bare now. Pins. Grease-pencil lines. Strings between settlements like a nervous system learning itself.

Admiral was lit. That was the news. The news had a carrier wave, and the carrier wave had been empty for months — static, a loop, one woman talking to weather. Then the calls started coming in.

Panel 1.2

A montage strip across the map's pins: a pump crew chief keying a handset in a drained basement; a lookout on the Admiral hall roof; a grandmother in a shoreline shelter holding a radio like a hymnal. Three mouths, three districts of static parting.

A pump crew. A hall full of fed people. A lookout who'd watched the substation mast take the signal and blink. Voices, where there had been one voice. Each completed district added mouths to Rae's once-empty radio.

Panel 1.3

Rae at the microphone, mid-broadcast, half-smiling despite herself. On the desk: a notebook where she has started writing down what the settlements call the man who walked out of Alki — the entries do not agree with each other.

RAE (radio): "Say your name and your street. The net holds who answers."

A light means nothing if nobody answers it. People were answering. And every answer carried a description of him, and no two descriptions matched, and the composite was becoming a person the city could ask for by name.

Panel 1.4

The café doorway, rain beyond. Ian stands just inside the light's edge, listening to a stranger's voice on the speaker describe a giant, a ghost, a saint — the stories already outrunning the scarred, dripping man in the actual doorway.

He had come ashore as a set of coordinates and a debt. Now he was a rumor with a route map. Rumors get asked to do things. Rumors get blamed at scale.

Panel 1.5

CLOSE on the map: a new pin going in at the Junction, Rae's hand steady, the string trembling. Ian's silhouette crosses the glass of the door behind her, unnoticed, going out into the rain to earn the next one.

The city was learning his name. Names are weight. Admiral had taught him how to hold weight for other people. It had not mentioned that his own name would be some of it.

PAGE 2 — HOLDING WEIGHT

Panel 2.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the Admiral substation, days after the restart — Ian braced in the pressure door the way this district now expects him to be, the vent crew moving through the gap his body makes, steam and rain and the grid humming awake around all of them.

Admiral's lesson, kept: strength is a thing other people stand under. The district had taken to scheduling its emergencies around his shoulders.

Panel 2.2

A drowned stairwell in an Admiral tower: a beam has come down across the only dry steps. Ian holds it — not lifting, holding, the distinction his whole life now — while a family crosses beneath with their entire world in grocery bags, the smallest child walking under his arm like a doorway that loves her.

He holds the beam for eleven minutes. It is not the hardest thing he does that week. It is the thing the district will tell stories about, because everyone in it understood it at a glance.

Panel 2.3

CLOSE: the vent chief checks the breaker housing and waits — everyone waits — for Ian's left arm on the contact, the arm with the white, branching burn up it under the jacket cuff. Routine now. A liturgy of the burned man and the patient machine.

The scar branches white against the tattoos. He wears it the way the district wears its grid: as proof that something was held closed until it was safe to let go.

Panel 2.4

The substation rail at shift's end. Radio chatter washes over the plot table — and one call cuts through, young and fast and coming from the Junction's roofs: a courier's voice, asking for the walker by name, with work attached.

Three districts had claims on him already. The fourth was calling. In the Junction, a sixteen-year-old owned the only roads that mattered — and she did not give them away to men too big for her roofs.

PAGE 3 — THREE SECONDS

Panel 3.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the gold-lit community hall — long tables, real food, people eating like people. On the wall, the map: a grease-pencil line drawn to a boundary labeled by a shaking hand: HIGH POINT PERIMETER. On a shelf, the hall's radio, mid-static.

The perimeter was on the map now. Not reached. Not saved. On the map. In the sealed city, that is what a horizon is: a line somebody drew because the alternative was not drawing it.

Panel 3.2

The static tears — just for a moment, the way a face surfaces in dark water. The whole hall hears it. Every spoon stops.

MISSY (radio, fragmented): "—keep walking—"

Three seconds. Her voice, through a failing grid and three districts of rain. Then the static closed over it like the Sound over a stone.

Panel 3.3

Ian, already standing. He does not remember standing. Around him the hall is very carefully not looking at him, the way you don't look at a man hearing his orders from God.

She had heard him and could not answer — that was the old sentence, the one the whole walk lived inside. Now she had answered. Three seconds of answer, and the grid ate the rest, and it was enough to rebuild him out of.

Panel 3.4

FULL-BLEED: Ian on the hall steps in the rain, the lit windows behind him, his face turned toward the fog where the perimeter line on the map says a woman is keeping a district alive on fumes.

He does. He keeps walking. It was never an instruction. It was a hand on the back of his neck, three seconds long, from the only person whose orders he has never once refused.

PAGE 4 — THE OLD MAN WITH THE PENCIL

Panel 4.1

HERO IMAGE (above): a shelter room at night, survivors asleep in rows. At a side table, KEITH — seventy-two, a teacher's posture worn into the bone of him — writes in a battered ledger by lamplight, a small radio murmuring beside his elbow.

There was a man in the sealed city who walked between the factions unarmed and unafraid, and every gate let him through, because he carried nothing anyone could steal except the truth about their own names.

Panel 4.2

CLOSE on the ledger: page after page of names in pencil — the lost, in a schoolteacher's hand, each one written like it might still be called on in class. A mug of water. A stub of pencil worn to a splinter.

The book was the lost. Every name he could learn, he wrote down. Pencil, not ink. The whole city knew about the book. The whole city had a theory about the pencil.

Panel 4.3

A girl from the shelter cots, awake, watching him write. The exchange happens the way it has happened a hundred times, and he answers it the way he has answered it a hundred times, without looking up.

GIRL: "Why pencil? Pencil fades."

KEITH: "Because I keep hoping to erase one."

Panel 4.4

The radio murmurs a name — the walker's, from the Junction's roofs, attached to work. Keith's pencil stops. He listens to the whole call. Then he closes the book, gently, the way you close a door on sleepers.

Some people keep the city in a ledger. Some keep it on their skin, in burns and bandages. The two bookkeepers had not met yet. The pencil had opinions about the skin. It was saving them.

PAGE 5 — CALIFORNIA AVENUE

Panel 5.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the Junction from the rooftops — California Avenue at dusk, storefronts and awnings, a stalled bus across the lanes, fog in the side streets, small armed figures owning the street level, and above them a whole second city: roofs, antennas, laundry lines, vents.

The Junction. Bandits held the street. An Apex hunted the dusk as the light drained. And mid-block, behind glass, sat the medicine half the peninsula was quietly dying without.

Panel 5.2

Street level through a rain-streaked awning: a bandit crew at a checkpoint of carts and wire, checking faces, taxing passage — Danny's order, or something wearing its shape. A horn sounds somewhere — a Runner pack moving blocks away.

The street was a toll road with better costumes. Everyone paid: in goods, in information, in looking at the ground the right way.

Panel 5.3

Ian on a parapet, reading the district the way he used to read rooms: exits, sightlines, weight. His eyes go up, past the awnings, to the roofs — where a strip of white cloth snaps on an antenna, deliberate as a flag.

Streets belong to the dead and the men who taxed them. But there was a second map above the street, drawn in cloth and bent antennas, and somebody maintained it like a garden.

Panel 5.4

Dusk deepening. On the roofs across the avenue, a small fast silhouette crosses a gap without breaking stride and is gone — a courier's silhouette, there and not there.

Nia Brooks had the medicine routes and a road toward Missy, and she ran them at the speed of a girl who had outrun the end of the world once already. First, he had to earn her roofs.

PAGE 6 — ROOF LANGUAGE

Panel 6.1

HERO IMAGE (above): NIA BROOKS on the roof — sixteen, braids, worn running gear, a courier's total economy of motion. Two fingers point the next roof. Beside her, the white cloth on its antenna snaps in the wet wind like something with a pulse.

Sixteen years old. A track star, once, in a world with tracks. Now the Junction's fastest scout, and the future the adults kept saying they were fighting for — she was tired of being a symbol. She preferred being a route.

Panel 6.2

Ian comes up the last vent ladder, huge and dripping, onto her roof. She looks him over the way a ferryman looks at weather. Her assessment is not flattering and she does not soften it.

NIA: "Streets belong to the dead. Roofs belong to whoever can keep moving."

NIA: "You look like weather. Can weather keep moving?"

Panel 6.3

The lesson, at speed, her finger stabbing marks across the block: a white strip on a vent, an antenna bent like a broken finger, a bare stretch of roof with nothing at all.

NIA: "White cloth, safe. Bent antenna, jump. No mark—"

IAN: "Listen."

NIA: "You learn fast."

Panel 6.4

She runs the first gap to show him — light, certain, gone before the eye finishes the sentence — and lands already turning to watch him measure it with a big man's honest doubt.

The Junction teaches him to move at somebody else's speed. Her speed was a language of marks and nerve, and fluency was measured in not falling. Class began at dusk. Dusk was when the street woke up.

Panel 6.5

CLOSE: Ian's scarred hand grips the parapet's wet edge, gauging the gap the way men gauge things they intend to survive. Below, the street and its toll-takers. Above, a girl waiting with her arms crossed, timing him.

He jumped. It was not graceful. Grace was a tax he had never been able to pay. But the roof held, and she nodded once, the way teachers do at a first correct answer.

PAGE 7 — AWNINGS

Panel 7.1

HERO IMAGE (above): Ian stretched along the wet spine of the roofs, following Nia's marks from vent to antenna, the dark avenue falling away below him, his bulk folded down to the smallest silhouette a man his size can rent.

Follow the route without touching street level. That was the whole of the law. The awnings below were a rumor of a floor — some would hold a man, some were painted canvas over air.

Panel 7.2

Ian tests a striped awning with one scarred hand, feels it sigh, and goes around by the parapet instead. A white cloth strip flutters approval from a vent.

He knew which ones lied because a shopkeeper had told him — water passed through security glass, a kindness with directions in it, on his first pass through the Junction. He still carried the bottle she had given him. He would carry it a while yet.

Panel 7.3

A bent antenna: the jump mark. Ian crosses to a lower roof in a shower of rain off the ledge, lands in a crouch that costs him his dignity and nothing else. From the street below: no shout, no shot. The roofs kept their secret.

Below, the toll-men taxed the ground. Above, two people crossed their district like weather crossing a map — briefly, and without permission.

Panel 7.4

Nia waits on the pharmacy block's high roof, silhouetted against the last of the light, one hand raised: stop. Below her mark, a skylight — black glass, the pharmacy's dark heart beneath it.

NIA: "Medicine's under us. Bandits are under that."

Big men do not belong on roofs. She knew it. She had let him up anyway. That was the Junction's whole foreign policy: the roof decides, and the roof had decided to see what he was for.

PAGE 8 — PHARMACY GLASS

Panel 8.1

The skylight from above: black glass beaded with rain, and below it the pharmacy's aisles in grainy dark — shelves of other people's survival, ordered by need, guarded by scarcity. Ian's reflection kneels on the glass like a ghost applying for entry.

Insulin. Antibiotics. The cold-chain bag that would keep them alive as far as Morgan. In the sealed city, a pharmacy was a bank, a church, and an argument, all with the same locked door.

Panel 8.2

Ian drops through the skylight on a knotted line into the dark among the shelves, silent as snowfall, reaching — while through the front glass, far at the store's mouth, flashlight beams begin to sweep: bandits, coming in the loud way.

The medicine mattered more than the noise. It usually does. He took the insulin first and the antibiotics second and his time about both, because hands that hurry in the dark are how the sealed city fills its cots.

Panel 8.3

CLOSE: the cold-chain bag filling — vials nested like eggs, his huge scarred hands absurdly gentle. On the top shelf, a child's drawing taped to the pharmacy's own register: a house, a sun, figures holding hands. He has seen this drawing before, in a café in Alki. The city keeps redrawing it.

Every district drew the same picture. House. Sun. Hands. The war was about whether the picture got to come true anywhere, ever, for anyone.

Panel 8.4

Above, through the skylight's wet glass: a muzzle-flash strobing on the next roof — no: a crash, glass, the sound of Nia's route coming apart at the seams. Ian's head comes up. The flashlight beams below swing toward the noise.

Below, bandits, turning toward the sound. Above, the sound itself, in a voice he knew. Dusk was done asking politely.

PAGE 9 — THE SHOPKEEPER

Panel 9.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the back-alley service door of a corner shop, seen from inside the dark: thick security glass, and behind it MRS. OKAFOR — apron still on, standing the way she stood for thirty years of customers, both palms pressed flat to the glass like she's waiting to be served by the world that ended.

He came out the pharmacy's back way into the alley — the extraction leg Nia had scouted — and the alley had a shop on it. He had known the shop. That was the problem. He had known the shop.

Panel 9.2

Memory-panel, softer rain: the same glass in an earlier week — her eyes kind above a mask of caution, a water bottle passed through the security slot, her finger pointing up: the blue awnings hold, the striped ones lie. Ian's hand taking the bottle like it was communion.

She had given him water through the glass and told him which awnings would hold his weight. It was the Junction's whole kindness in one transaction: everything through glass, nothing wasted, directions included.

Panel 9.3

Now. Ian stands in the wet alley with the medicine bag on his shoulder and looks at her through the glass for exactly as long as respect requires and survival allows. She does not know him. She does not know anyone. The palms stay flat.

The palms flat like she's waiting for a customer. She is. Some part of the machinery still believes in opening hours, in regulars, in the man who'd come back for the bottle someday.

Panel 9.4

CLOSE: the water bottle — her bottle, carried since she gave it — set down on the shop's step, full, upright, in the rain. Ian's hand leaving the frame. The door stays shut.

He leaves the water bottle on the step. He doesn't go in. Some doors you keep shut out of respect for who opened them before — and because she would have wanted the shop kept, the way she kept it: locked, stocked, and kind through glass.

PAGE 10 — ONE GOOD LEG

Panel 10.1

The pharmacy roof, minutes later, dark coming down hard: the extraction has gone loud — bandits at both ends of the block, fire on the street stairs, the skylight line the only way out, and Nia on the high roof covering it with a thrown flare and a courier's nerve.

Routes converge the way rivers do: violently, and at the worst ground available. The medicine was up. She was the ladder it climbed by.

Panel 10.2

Nia hit — the panel refuses spectacle: just her hand slapping flat on wet tar-paper, her leg folding wrong under her, her face turned to the sky, furious at the geometry of it. Her voice comes out level, the way it comes out on the radio.

NIA: "Leg's done. Route's not."

She was hit extracting the medicine — doing the city's arithmetic with her own body as the chalk. Sixteen years old, and her first thought was the route. The city should be ashamed of what it teaches its children. It isn't. That's why it needs them.

Panel 10.3

Ian gets her across his shoulders without a word — the fireman's carry, her weight settled, her hands free, the medicine bag passed to her grip because carrying is a team event now.

NIA: "You can't carry me and fight."

IAN: "Watch."

Panel 10.4

WIDE: the two of them against the dusk — a huge man with a girl across his shoulders at the roof's edge, the largest weapons left behind in the pharmacy dark, one UV lamp in his free hand like a candle against the whole night.

He could not use his largest weapons while carrying her. What he had left was a lamp, one hand, and her eyes — and the Junction, which had taught him to move at somebody else's speed, was about to grade the exam at a run.

PAGE 11 — HER SPEED

Panel 11.1

The carry, first roof: Ian moving under her weight with his stride completely rearranged — shorter, lower, listening. Nia rides high, scanning, calling the roof like a coxswain calls a river.

NIA: "Bent one next. Jump on my word. My word, not your nerve."

He moves at her speed now. That was the district's lesson and the carry was the classroom: a man who had only ever set his own pace, taking his tempo from a sixteen-year-old with one good leg.

Panel 11.2

A crossing in rain over a laundry-line bridge of boards and rope — below, bandits flowing along the avenue they own, torches and tarps, unaware of the shadow passing three storeys up with its double heartbeat.

Below, the street taxed the ground. Above, the cargo was a person and the vehicle was a person, and the toll for the crossing was total quiet and a shoulder that had started, already, to plan its complaint.

Panel 11.3

Nia navigating from memory, upside down to the world: vent, cloth, gap, the hotel sign's dead frame — her map unrolling ahead of his feet, each call arriving exactly one step before it was needed.

NIA: "Vent. Cloth. Gap. Trust the gap."

He is the legs. She is the map. Neither works alone, and the Junction had arranged the lesson so that admitting it was the only way home. He admitted it with every step.

Panel 11.4

Both of them freeze mid-roof. Ahead, quartering the rooftops on all fours in the last light, a pale shape — an Apex, hunting the dusk, head swinging like a dog casting for scent. Nia's whisper is barely weather.

NIA: "Stop talking."

He hadn't been. But he understood: it was her way of saying the part where their lives depended on his stillness had arrived, and she wanted it on the record that she was the calm one.

PAGE 12 — THE PARAPET

Panel 12.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the roof narrows to a parapet run — and the Apex comes over the edge into the frame, pale and wet and patient, while Ian works the UV lamp one-handed, Nia across his shoulders, her hands locked in his jacket, the violet light steaming where it strikes wet concrete.

Nowhere to set her down. Nowhere to put the lamp down. The parapet was a sentence with no spare words, and the thing climbing into it intended to edit them both.

Panel 12.2

The UV worked like a fencer's blade — feint, burn, feint — Ian's one free arm writing bright grammar in the rain while his other arm keeps her balanced through every lunge of the fight happening under her.

UV is a language Apex understand in their skin. He spoke it one-handed, in short sentences, because a long sentence would cost him his footing, and his footing was carrying a person.

Panel 12.3

Nia's voice from above his head, steady as a metronome, calling the footing she cannot see him take — reading the roof by the sway of his shoulders, the way sailors read weather by the mast.

NIA: "Left edge holds. Trust me."

He trusts her. The edge holds. The thing goes back over the parapet the way it came, carrying its burns like a review of the evening. Trust, in the Junction, is a load-bearing material.

Panel 12.4

After: rain again, just rain. Ian still standing in the fighting crouch a moment too long, Nia still aboard, both of them breathing like a bellows with two chambers.

NIA: "You're supposed to breathe during."

IAN: "Noted."

PAGE 13 — THE STRANDED BUS

Panel 13.1

The roof route dead-ends at a collapsed stair tower — and below, spanning the avenue like a beached ship, the stranded evacuation bus: roof to roof, the only bridge left over the bandit street. Its roof shines with rain, long and narrow as a gangplank.

The bus had died full of other people's escapes, in another life. Tonight it was infrastructure: sixty feet of wet steel between the roofs that were safe and the roofs that were next.

Panel 13.2

The crossing: Ian on the bus roof under his double weight, boots drumming hollow on the wet metal — and in the lanes below, Runners filling the street like a river rising, reaching up the bus's flanks at the sound.

The street belonged to the dead. The bus belonged to whoever could keep moving. Every step rang. Every ring of it drew the lanes fuller, the way a bell draws a town.

Panel 13.3

Halfway, the bus shifts on its suspension — a long groan, a tilt of two degrees that feels like twenty — and Nia's hands tighten, and her voice goes to the metronome she used on the parapet, counting him across like a man defusing the ground itself.

NIA: "Slow is fast. Slow is fast. Slow—"

She counts his steps because hers are done for the night and somebody's have to be counted by somebody. That is the whole social contract of the sealed city, on a bus roof, in the rain: your steps, my count, our crossing.

Panel 13.4

The far roof: Ian's boot on tar-paper, the bus behind them settling back into its grave of traffic, the lanes below still boiling. Nia looks back once at the shining hull they'd crossed.

NIA: "Put that in the book. Bus roof. My call."

It would go in every book the Junction kept — hers, Rae's, eventually an old man's in pencil. Routes are just stories that hold weight. This one now held a man, a girl, and the medicine half a district was waiting on.

PAGE 14 — THE GAP

Panel 14.1

The last gap: the extraction roof across a service alley, tar-paper and lamplight and waiting hands — too far. Farther than a jump. Much farther than a jump carrying a person, and both of them do the arithmetic at the same moment and arrive at the same ugly sum.

Every route in the Junction ends at a gap that was measured for one body. The route had not been designed by anyone who imagined the courier would be cargo.

Panel 14.2

Nia reads his face, reads the gap, and makes the decision with the serene authority of a girl who has been making it all night about everything.

NIA: "Do it right, old man."

She is not afraid of the throw. She is afraid of being set down gently and left, the way cargo gets left when the math turns. She has met the world. She prefers the throw, and him, and says so with four words.

Panel 14.3

The throw — and mid-motion, off the fire escape below, a Runner takes its payment: a ribbon of skin off Ian's shoulder, the price of the arc his body draws to launch her true. She crosses the gap like a thrown spear of a girl, straight and certain.

He throws her across the final gap and the city charges him for the gesture on the spot, in skin. The bandage on that shoulder will stay for two districts, graying, re-tied every morning. It starts here, as a red line drawn by a dead thing's hand.

Panel 14.4

Caught — the far roof erupts in hands: blankets, the medicine bag passed up hand over hand like a bucket at a fire, Nia already propped on an elbow, already directing her own rescue's paperwork.

NIA: "Bag first. Then me. Bag first."

Bag first. Sixteen years old, one leg a ruin, mid-air a moment ago — and her triage is flawless and her priorities are the route's. The Junction's future, ladies and gentlemen, is in savage good hands.

Panel 14.5

Ian comes across last, by rope and nerve, and lands in the lamplight among the extraction crew — blood running bright down his arm, the girl watching his shoulder with a new, permanent attentiveness being born in her face.

Nia learns to check the bandage without asking. It starts tonight, in lamplight, with a look neither of them comments on. Some debts get paid in inspections, every morning, for two districts.

PAGE 15 — WHAT WE LEAVE

Panel 15.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the rooftop café's back room, lamplight and rain — Nia on a bench with her leg propped and splinted, Ian seated while an old survivor ties the strip of cloth around his torn shoulder, and on the floor between them, two open crates: medicine, and demolition caps, gleaming like a decision.

Extraction. The word sounds clean. It is a room full of bleeding people, a girl trying not to cry from a leg she refuses to look at, and a choice that has to be made before dawn with wet hands.

Panel 15.2

Nia, pale as paper, glaring at Ian like the whole evening is personally his fault — which, in the ways that matter to a sixteen-year-old, it is.

NIA: "You said 'watch.' I watched. You almost dropped the lamp."

IAN: "Almost."

NIA: "Do better with the next cripple."

Panel 15.3

The crates, closer: one road's worth of carrying capacity left before dawn. The medicine goes south to Morgan's clinic — to cots with names on them. The caps go east to Delridge — demolition, a loud road opened by force. Both are needed. One can be carried.

Choose medicine for Morgan or demolition caps for Delridge. The sealed city runs on choices like this: whichever you carry, the other becomes a debt with a date on it.

Panel 15.4

Ian's hand settles on the medicine crate. It is not a dramatic gesture. It is a man picking up a box, which is what most of history actually looks like up close.

IAN: "Morgan gets the medicine."

Delridge would wait, and waiting has a price list too — it always does. He would see this one's invoice soon, on cots, in a clinic where a woman kept the accounts in names.

Panel 15.5

Dawn over the Junction rooftops: rescued civilians moving into the café and the pharmacy roof, new rope bridges spanning the blocks, a district standing up out of its toll road. On the high roof, a white cloth snaps, fresh-tied.

The Junction was open. The city learned his name a second time — in a sixteen-year-old's voice, calling jumps in the dark, and in the sound of a man moving at somebody else's speed. Two districts had taught him. The third was a forest, and it taught the opposite of everything.

PAGE 16 — THE GREEN DARK

Panel 16.1

HERO IMAGE (above): Lincoln Park at night — towering wet cedars, black water beyond the bluff, and ELI COLE standing motionless under the trees with one hand raised, while between the trunks the infected stand asleep in the mist, heads bowed, dozens deepening into hundreds toward the shore.

Lincoln Park. The green dark. No camp, no walls, no permanent anything — Eli Cole had kept his people alive by refusing to be findable, and the park had kept its own counsel for months, in a voice just under hearing.

Panel 16.2

Eli, close: a hunting guide's face, weathered past age into landscape, eyes that taught Ian's father to shoot in another century of the world. He looks at Ian's size, Ian's bandage, Ian's noise, and his verdict is gentle and total.

ELI: "Gunfire here wakes all of it."

IAN: "How many?"

ELI: "You don't want the number."

Panel 16.3

The sleeping district, wider: infected standing in the wet between the cedars like a congregation at a paused hymn — ferrymen, joggers, whole picnic parties of the turned, preserved by the cold and the quiet and the discipline of the man who shares their woods.

They sleep standing, the way horses do, the way the neighborhood did everything now: in place, in the rain, waiting for a sound worth finishing the motion for.

Panel 16.4

Eli leads off along no visible path, his steps making less sound than the rain does. Ian follows, rearranging his huge body around the lesson, the UV lamp dark in his hand by order.

ELI: "The infected hunt noise. People hunt certainty. The woods give neither."

Admiral taught him to hold weight. The Junction taught him somebody else's speed. Lincoln Park's tuition was the third thing, the hardest: that killing is sometimes the loudest, worst solution — and the night would test whether he'd learned it, or only heard it.

PAGE 17 — THE HUSH

Panel 17.1

The grove of the dormant: rows of sleepers among the trunks, and strung between the trees at ankle and chest height, fishing lines hung with tin cans — a silver, silent web of other people's mistakes, each can a small bell that has already rung for somebody.

The Hush. Cross it wrong and the cans sing, and the grove wakes, and the grove is the size of a small town's dreams. Cross it right and you are a rumor the trees keep.

Panel 17.2

JEFF — the park's own guide, mid-forties, twitchy as a held breath — touching two fingers to a blaze mark on a cedar, then to the mud where his boot-print sits, the next already placed. His hands shake everywhere except on his own trails.

JEFF: "Step where I stepped. Only where I stepped."

Jeff knew every game path and drainage cut the green dark had. He was certain everyone leaves him, eventually, the way weather leaves. The trails were the one thing that had never left. He lent them out like sacraments.

Panel 17.3

Ian passes a sleeper at the distance of a held breath — close enough to see the rain beading on a dead man's ear, the grey bandage on his own shoulder ghosting in the mist — and his hand, the famous hand, stays open and empty and down.

A man who came ashore measuring every room for exits learns to measure himself for noise. Not reaching for the knife costs him more than any fight in Admiral. Restraint is a muscle. The park is its gymnasium.

Panel 17.4

The far side: Eli waiting under the last cedar, counting them through with his eyes the way a shepherd counts. Behind the party, the cans hang silent in their lines, unsung.

ELI: "Corridor stays open. Long as nobody's proud in it."

Somewhere behind them the grove keeps its counsel. A permanent quiet corridor stays open through the park at night — because no gun was fired in it, and no voice was raised, and a huge man walked through it like weather apologizing.

PAGE 18 — THE RANGER

Panel 18.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the north trail, rain in the cedars — and on the path, a park ranger standing the way the sleepers stand, uniform soaked dark, head bowed, a whistle still hanging on its lanyard against his chest. Ian a few paces off, stopped dead. Eli behind him, silent.

The ranger had warned Ian off the north trails, days into the new world, alive and exasperated and kind about it: they go quiet up there, he'd said, and quiet is worse.

Panel 18.2

Closer: the lanyard, the whistle, the badge's ghost under rain. The ranger walks these trails still — the panel shows the worn path his patrol has kept open through the blackberry, a groove in the green dark made by a man still doing his job at the level below thought.

He walks the same trails. The whistle is still on the lanyard. Whatever the park took, it did not take the route, and it did not take the rounds. There are worse things to be than a habit that outlives its man. There are not many sadder.

Panel 18.3

Ian stands there a long time. The efficient thing walks away, saves its minutes for the living. The man stays a moment longer, in the rain, at attention in nothing but posture — paying the toll the green dark actually charges.

He doesn't explain it to Eli. He has a list of men he walks around now — a deckhand at a ferry gate, a shopkeeper behind glass, a ranger on his rounds. The list is the walk, as much as any map.

Panel 18.4

Eli finds him standing there after, and for once says nothing at all — the old guide simply takes the trail again, slower than his own pace, so the younger man's moment can finish itself behind him.

In the green dark, silence is also a way of saying the names. Eli, who said almost nothing as a creed, said this one perfectly.

PAGE 19 — LOW GOLD

Panel 19.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the shoreline shelters at night — low hooded lamps glowing warm under their shields, pitched so no light spills toward the bluff; rope lines and pulleys strung between the posts; tents, a ruined dock, and Puget Sound going black beyond.

The work quiet makes possible: low gold. Lights that warm a camp without advertising it to the forest. In Lincoln Park, even hope has to keep its voice down.

Panel 19.2

Hands in lamplight: Ian and Eli's people rigging the shore camp — rope and pulleys salvaged from the ruined dock, a supply line that can move food over ground no cart survives. Jeff tests a knot three times, then a fourth, for the road's sake.

A ruined dock gives up its rope. A dead park gives up its paths. The sealed city is a salvage operation conducted by the bereaved, and everything in it is used twice, the way everything in it is mourned twice.

Panel 19.3

Two coils on the wet planks, lamplight between them: the long rope rig, promised west — to Westwood's evacuees, whose road out runs uphill through worse country than this. And the utility cable, which can feed Morgan's clinic and bind the districts into one body.

Give the rope to Westwood, or the cable to Morgan. The arithmetic again — it follows him like weather. He sends the cable to Morgan, where a doctor is keeping people alive by candlelight and arithmetic of her own. Westwood waits. Westwood will be billed for waiting, later, in a currency he already hates.

Panel 19.4

WIDE and quiet: the shore camp under its hooded lamps, the corridor through the trees behind it dark and open, the Sound in front of it black and patient. A held note of a place.

The shelters gained their low lights. The corridor stayed open. Lincoln Park had taught its lesson and given its gifts, and asked only the usual tuition, payable in skin — and the night, being the night, was already reaching for the collection plate.

PAGE 20 — THE STAND

Panel 20.1

The shelter line at the moment the quiet ends: a sound lure trips somewhere in the black — a bandit horn, a falling can-line, history will argue it — and between the cedars the standing sleepers begin, all at once, to be a direction.

Quiet has a terminus. It is always the same terminus: a sound, in the wrong place, from the wrong throat, and the green dark wakes in waves and comes downhill toward the little lamps like the tide deciding.

Panel 20.2

The stand: fire barrels lit, hooded lamps thrown open, benches and fencing dragged into a line — and in the line, exactly one gap, and the gap is exactly one man wide, because the shelters' whole defense was designed around the hope that it would never be needed.

Forty in the signature wave. Sixty at the cap. The numbers are Eli's, counted the way he counts everything: afterward, quietly, with the respect due to arithmetic that tried to kill you.

Panel 20.3

Ian in the gap with a rebar maul, silent, unhurried, a wall that bleeds — the wave breaking on him the way surf breaks, in pieces, with the pieces still coming. No gun. A gun would wake the whole park; a man can only wake the part of it already awake.

Lincoln Park taught him killing is sometimes the loudest, worst solution. He killed anyway. That is the whole of the lesson: sometimes the worst solution is the one standing between the wave and the lamps, and it does its work, and it does not get to feel clean about it.

Panel 20.4

CLOSE in the press: blackberry thorns and worse open his left cheek in a long line; one cut crosses his eyebrow and pulls it crooked. Blood and rain together. His expression does not change. The maul does not hurry.

Thorn lacerations across the left cheek. One scar cuts through his eyebrow and never heals straight. After this, strangers flinch at him first, and ask later. The park signs its work the way all the districts do: on his face, where he has to wear it into every room he will ever enter.

Panel 20.5

The wave, thinning. The lamps, still lit. Behind him the shelters' people hold their stretch of the line with boat-hooks and table legs and the discovery that they can. The gap holds. The man in it sways, once, like a tree deciding.

The stand holds because a district stood in it — that's the part the stories will leave out, and the part he'd insist on. He was the gap. They were the line. Lincoln Park kept its lamps, and sent him on to Morgan with its signature written across his face.

PAGE 21 — THE LOUD LESSON

Panel 21.1

HERO IMAGE (above): dawn the color of wet ash at the shore camp — smoke where the barrels were, survivors moving softly among the shelters, and Ian alone on a bench with the maul across his knees and the new cuts stiffening on his cheek, kept at the distance people keep from a stove that saved the house.

Afterward is its own district. It has no missions. You just live in it a while, while the adrenaline leaves and the arithmetic arrives.

Panel 21.2

Eli settles at the far end of the bench — the closest anyone sits to Ian that morning — and delivers the green dark's whole philosophy in the tone of a man reading a trail sign.

ELI: "Loud is a debt. You paid it for them."

ELI: "Spend the quiet better, next time."

Panel 21.3

A child from the shelters starts toward Ian with a cup of water, reads the camp's flinch in the adults around her — the new flinch, the one his face earns now — and hesitates. Ian sees it. Files it. Another receipt.

Strangers flinch at him first now, and ask later. It is the park's true tuition, and it is non-refundable: the face that stood in the gap becomes, to everyone who wasn't in it, the face of the gap itself.

Panel 21.4

The radio at the café, a world away and one district over, carrying Lincoln mouths now too — new call signs joining Rae's map. Ian, rising from the bench, the maul left behind for the camp like a tool returned to its shelf.

Three districts, three versions of strength — hold weight, take another's speed, spend quiet like it's yours. The city had his name in three accents now. All of them were true. None of them were the whole man. Ahead: the broken middle, where every road he'd built came to be audited by a woman with a clinic and a long memory.

PAGE 22 — THE BROKEN MIDDLE

Panel 22.1

HERO IMAGE (above): MORGAN JUNCTION at night in the rain — the clinic in its converted storefront, gold light in the windows, a queue of the hurt under the awning, the cargo lift standing ready, and Ian arriving out of the dark with the medicine crate on his shoulder and the cable crew's cable behind him.

Morgan Junction. The broken middle. Every route crossed here, and every supply became somebody's emergency the moment it arrived — including, especially, his.

Panel 22.2

The arrival the storyline promised: medicine from the Junction, cable from Lincoln — both. A quiet arrival, the good kind. It begins, anyway, in a triage crisis: three litters at the door at once, Sora's voice from inside triaging by sound before sight.

Entering with both is a quiet arrival. Quiet is relative. In Morgan, quiet means only three emergencies at the door instead of five, and a doctor who has already decided which one is yours to watch.

Panel 22.3

CLOSE, easy to miss: the clinic yard's side gate — Danny's-side gate, the camp-logistics gate every clinic keeps chained by regulation and by Sora's personal law — standing unlatched. Ian passes through it, stops, looks at the latch a moment. Latches it behind him. Says nothing.

Somebody had left the Morgan gate open for him. Somebody inside the camp's own logistics, with a steady hand and a reason. He would not learn who for a long time. Nia, arriving with the second crate, saw the latch too — and filed it, the way couriers file everything, against a day it might mean something.

Panel 22.4

Inside at last: gold light, cots, the queue of the hurt — and DR. SORA KIM working without looking up, her hands already in the next problem, her voice arriving before her eyes do.

SORA: "Crate down. Hands where I can see them. Then stand there."

Every route converged at her clinic. Every decision he'd made was about to be introduced to him formally — lying down, looking up, with names attached.

PAGE 23 — STAY FOR THE NAMES

Panel 23.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the clinic ward, lamplight and cots — Sora with her board under one arm, walking Ian down the row like a docent of consequences, while the ward breathes and drips and hurts around them at conversational volume.

She made him stay. Not for thanks — Morgan didn't trade in it — and not for punishment, which she considered a waste of a teaching hospital. For the names. It was a curriculum. He was the only student.

Panel 23.2

Cot one: a young man with a bandaged head, sitting up against orders — the Alki lookout, the frightened boy from the bandit skiff whom Ian had talked past a gun instead of through one. Alive. Grinning weakly at the giant in the doorway like at a weather event that spared his house.

SORA: "Micah Anson. The skiff lookout. Nineteen. You left him breathing, so he gets to be nineteen."

A decision, lying on a cot, looking at him. This one had come out kind. The row was long, and kindness was not its average.

Panel 23.3

Cot two: a mother asleep with her child curled into the dry side of the bed — an Admiral family, from the clinic circuit; their basement was the one the pumps drained while Ian held the district's weight. The child's feet are dry. It is an enormous detail. It is the whole detail.

SORA: "The Adeyemis. Her boy's chest is clear because a basement dried. She doesn't know your name. The pumps do."

Admiral's weight, converted: one family's lungs. The arithmetic of the walk, done in strangers, most of whom would never know the exchange rate.

Panel 23.4

Cot three, the light lower: a woman turned half to the wall, fever working her like weather, a Junction civilian — a name from a street Ian crossed — infected during a delay: a route chosen, an hour spent elsewhere, a bite collected in the margin of his arithmetic.

SORA: "Ruth Calloway. Bitten during the delay on California Avenue. Your delay. Stay for the names, Ian."

Every route converged at her clinic. The Alki lookout he'd spared. The Admiral family. The woman his delay cost. Medicine is hope measured in doses — and she made him stay while the doses were counted out in people.

Panel 23.5

CLOSE: Ian's face doing nothing at all, which on Ian is a shout. Sora watches him take it without flinching from any of the three cots, and something in her accounting of him adjusts itself, permanently.

SORA: "Most men count supplies. You'll do. You'll do because you count wrong on purpose — people first, and it costs you."

He doesn't answer. There is nothing in his eight words for this. She seems to count even that in his favor, and moves him along the row like inventory she has decided to keep.

PAGE 24 — THE SAME CURRENCY

Panel 24.1

The clinic corridor, the small hours: the triage crisis has a tail — a bandit probe at the yard door, knife-work in the choke point, Ian between it and the ward with the UV dark and his hands full of a problem that bleeds.

It ends the way corridor fights end: quickly, badly, and in the wrong body. A bandit knife opens his thigh on the ward side of the door. The door holds. The ward never wakes. That was the entire objective, and it was met, and it is not the same as free.

Panel 24.2

Sora stitching the thigh wound in the corridor under a work lamp, flat and furious, while he stands there taking up the whole doorway — too big to sit in her space, too stubborn to lean, being repaired like a door himself.

She works the way she accounts: without waste, without anesthesia for the feelings, naming each stitch's purpose as she goes, because a man who pays in this currency should at least get an itemized receipt.

Panel 24.3

CLOSE on her hands, steady; his scarred fist opening, slowly, on purpose, as the needle goes through — restraint practiced even here, even now, at the level of a single hand.

SORA: "You keep paying in the same currency."

He doesn't argue. There is an argument — the ward slept, the door held, the children in the cots kept their arithmetic simple — and he leaves it unspoken, because she knows it, and because unspoken is where he keeps all his best evidence.

Panel 24.4

Ian walking the ward one last time that night, uneven now — the thigh's new gait, a limp the length of a district arriving in his stride — past the three cots, past all the cots, a giant doing rounds on a hospital he isn't staff of.

He walks uneven for a full district after. The body keeps the ledger the pencil can't: burn, bandage, cheek, thigh. Every district leaves its mark on him, in order. He is becoming a heavily annotated man.

PAGE 25 — THE FIELD KIT

Panel 25.1

HERO IMAGE (above): Sora's office, lamplight — the field kit on the desk between them: sealed, rugged, latched, with a gate tag wired to its handle. Her ledger lies open beside it, and the ledger's argument is the kit's price.

The kit was a stabilized field unit, keyed and coded — the thing that opens High Point's inner gate, the last locked door between Ian and the person at the end of the walk. Sora had held it through the whole war like a verdict waiting for a defendant worth it.

Panel 25.2

Before the kit, the accounting that earns it: the clinic's last antibiotics, three doses, more claimants than doses — and then the long inventory recovered, bag by tagged bag, until the shelf could be generous again. Trust, in Morgan, is a stock level.

Three doses, and the choosing, and the finding of more — that was his entrance examination, and he had passed it the slow way: by staying for the names until the names became a stockroom.

Panel 25.3

The kit crossing the desk — her hands letting go, his scarred hands taking the weight with the exact care he'd used on insulin vials, on a girl across his shoulders, on everything the war had ever handed him that mattered.

SORA: "This opens her inner gate. The bill comes with it."

IAN: "Name it."

SORA: "Remember everyone."

Panel 25.4

FULL-BLEED: Ian in the clinic doorway at dawn, kit in hand, limp and all, the gold-lit ward behind him and the rising road to High Point ahead, where a perimeter line on a café map waits to become a place.

Every road out of Morgan rose toward High Point. The kit was the key. The names were the lock it turned in him. And somewhere across the wet districts, on a frequency that wasn't Rae's, a reasonable man was about to make the city the best offer it had ever heard — and mean it as a cage.

PAGE 26 — THE OPPOSING ARGUMENT

Panel 26.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the café at night, the radio on its table at the room's center — everyone in frame listening, no one touching it, the dial's weak glow the only fire in the room. A calm voice is coming out of the speaker, and the room is giving it the respect due to artillery.

The frequency wasn't Rae's. It threaded the relays like it owned them — intercepted, rebroadcast, unstoppable — a voice the city had heard in fragments for months, arriving now at full length, on purpose.

Panel 26.2

CLOSE on the speaker grille; around it, the listeners' faces in candlelight — a pump-crew chief, a Junction runner, Ian in the back with his new limp and his old stillness. Nobody writes anything down. Nobody has to.

DANNY (radio): "The seal is mercy. The outside will burn this peninsula the moment it opens. I only ask High Point for the keys — so no one has to die proving it."

The first time the whole city heard Danny at length: calm, warm, reasonable. The voice of a man offering shelter from a fire he describes beautifully. He never raised it. He never had to. Fear does its own volume.

Panel 26.3

The room's doubt, drawn plainly: a woman looking at her sleeping child in the café's corner; an old man looking at the door, at the rain, at the direction of the bridge — doing the offer's math in his face, finding it comes out even.

The hell of it: he is not wrong about the risk. The outside wrote them off. The seal kept the fire out — so far. An argument doesn't have to be false to be a cage. It just has to be the only one with a transmitter.

Panel 26.4

Ian, in the back, saying nothing, learning the enemy the way he learns everything: by standing still inside its weather. Rae at the desk, already calculating what the net answers a voice like that with.

He offered High Point power — real power, grid power, the thing Missy's people were freezing in the dark without — in exchange for Westlight's radio keys. It was, everyone in the room understood, a very good offer. That was the atrocity of it.

Panel 26.5

The radio alone for a beat after the broadcast ends, the room still not touching it, the café light burning in the window behind the glass like a thesis statement.

Missy refused. Her grid was failing anyway. That's what made it a good offer — and her refusal, up the hill in the brownout, the act of a woman who understood that some keys are the city itself, and do not get sold for light.

PAGE 27 — THE REFUSAL

Panel 27.1

HERO IMAGE (above): HIGH POINT's grid room under brownout — MISSY at the breaker panel, one hand on a switch, a radio handset at her ear, the panel's lights dying in sequence behind her hand like a row of small surrenders she is personally refusing to sign.

Cutaway — because this volume is also hers. Before Ian ever arrives, High Point is a woman holding a roof up with one hand and a grid together with the other, in the dark, on fumes, at the speed of triage.

Panel 27.2

The offer, replayed on speaker for the room — Danny wanted witnesses, and got them: residents in the doorway, a child, Samir's people at the relays. Her grid is failing audibly; a freezer bank gives up somewhere below with a sigh like a held breath let go.

He offered her people light and heat and time. All of it real. All of it priced in a single currency: the keys — whoever holds Westlight's keys holds the only trusted signal, and whoever holds the signal holds the city's story of itself.

Panel 27.3

Her people's faces: afraid of the dark, afraid of the cold stores, and — newest fear, the one Danny's voice was really selling — afraid of the walk: of the man coming up the hill through three districts like a siege with a name, and the war his road might bring to their gate.

They were afraid Ian's approach would bring a war. They weren't wrong to be afraid. The war was already coming up the hill. It was just also bringing medicine, and a field kit, and three districts of witnesses. Fear edits. It always cuts the second half of the sentence.

Panel 27.4

Missy's hand on the transmitter key. Her face calm the way deep water is calm. She gives the answer on the open channel, so the whole peninsula can hold her to it.

MISSY (radio): "The keys stay here. So does the light."

She refused a working grid in a drowning district to keep a promise about a signal. Three districts away, a man with a new limp heard the brownout inside her voice — and the walk, which had been a duty with a woman's name on it, became a debt coming due at speed.

PAGE 28 — THE DEAD DROP

Panel 28.1

HERO IMAGE (above): a rusted tin under a bridge piling in the rain — Ian's scarred hand drawing out a folded note while, out of focus on a rooftop behind him, a woman with long dark hair watches, and does not wave, and is gone before the focus could change its mind.

The drops had been coming for weeks. A tin, a piling, a page of rotations in a hand that shook only in the writing. Sara Lindgren. His first love. Now standing at Danny's side — feeding Ian the truth, one drop at a time.

Panel 28.2

The note's contents as Ian reads them by flashlight in the lee of the piling: patrol rotations, span charge placements, timings in a dispatcher's shorthand — professional, complete, the work of a woman who had decided exactly what her life was for now.

Span charge placements. Patrol rotations. The demolition rig's habits. It was the bridge, handed to him a page at a time, by the person the camp believed belonged to the man on the mask.

Panel 28.3

The intel working — a patrol avoided by four minutes in the rain; a cache found exactly where the shorthand said; a route re-drawn on Rae's map in grease pencil, in Ian's hand, growing more confident by the week.

It worked. That was the hell of it — it worked every time. A plan built on her drops began to draw itself on the map in confident lines: spans, rotations, the Counterweight rig. Ian's bridge, designed by a ghost at the enemy's shoulder.

Panel 28.4

The rooftop, empty now, rain erasing the place where she stood. Ian folds the note into the tin's twin — his own archive, carried against his ribs — and goes down into the dark to be a plan's legs.

Everything she passes is true. Everything. He believes it because it's earned. She believes it because she's the one passing it. Remember that she believes it too. It matters, where this road bends.

PAGE 29 — THE GHOST AT HIS SHOULDER

Panel 29.1

Danny's camp from above — fire barrels, tarps, the bridge approach's shadow across it all — and at its center a tall figure in a respirator mask, seen only from behind and above, reading a patrol report by firelight. The face is never shown. The mask never comes off. The camp orbits him like weather.

The camp thought in orbits. At its center: a longshoreman's ledger, a bridge crew's respirator, and a man who had watched cars die on a span and decided that obedience's body count would be answered by ownership. He is not crazy. That is what makes him dangerous.

Panel 29.2

Sara at his shoulder, pouring, close the way the camp reads as his — her face arranged into the expression of a woman who belongs to the arrangement. Under his arm, the waterlogged ledger. Somewhere in it, her name is a line item with a balance.

The camp thought she was his. The truth: Danny held her life in his ledger, and she had decided to spend it on warnings. It is the longest performance of her life, and she is forgetting where it ends — which is exactly where he keeps her.

Panel 29.3

At the fire's edge: ROOK — the lieutenant, ex-PD, the steady hand of Danny's logistics — watching Sara not look at the patrol report she already knows by heart. His face does the arithmetic of a man holding a truth he hasn't spent yet, and hating the interest it earns.

Rook held a truth, too — about gates left open, about which pages of the flow were salted. He was the counter-intelligence correction, walking around in the enemy's camp with his badge in his pocket and his oath in his head, in that order. Whether he ever spent it was a coin still spinning.

Panel 29.4

Later, alone in a stockroom's dark: Sara folding another note, her hands shaking so hard the paper rattles — the performance off, the woman underneath it counting her own pulse like a rotation schedule.

Every dead drop could be the one he's been waiting for. Her intel might be buying her life — or her execution, pre-written and filed under her own name in his book. She folds the note anyway. It is the only sentence she gets to finish anymore.

Panel 29.5

The masked figure again, from behind, closing the ledger on a page the firelight doesn't reach. The report in his other hand — the true one. The one he'll salt.

The deeper cut: Danny had known for weeks. He let the real intel flow to earn her trust. Then he started feeding her lies to pass along — true things, wrapped around one lie, like a pill in food. And the lie had a specific address, and a specific dawn, picked out for Ian Bronson personally.

PAGE 30 — EAST SPAN — DEAD

Panel 30.1

HERO IMAGE (above): the café's back room as a war room — the bridge diagram spread on the table in grease pencil and confidence: spans, rotations, the Counterweight rig's anchor points, a dozen hands at the diagram's edges, the folded dead-drop note weighting one corner like a paperweight with a pulse.

The plan, assembled from a ghost's handwriting: how to come at the bridge, when the patrols thin, where the spans can be cut and where they must be held. A good plan. A true plan. Ninety percent of one — and in demolition work, the other ten percent is the whole story.

Panel 30.2

Over the diagram, the room's new gravity: Rae's net feeding timings, the Junction's runners volunteering for the high work, Morgan's medic already packing for a bridge — the districts, which had been audiences for his name, becoming an operation around it.

Three districts of voices on the radio. A clinic's ledger of the living. A park's rope and a corridor of quiet. This is what the city learning his name was for: not the stories. The muster.

Panel 30.3

CLOSE on the diagram's east span — and above it, in Sara's dispatcher shorthand, the annotation that does the quietest work in the whole volume: EAST SPAN CHARGES — DEAD. Ian's scarred finger rests beside it, trusting it completely, the way you trust a load-bearing wall.

One annotation. Four words, in the handwriting of the bravest person in the enemy's camp, who believed them with her whole heart because the man who fed them to her had spent weeks making sure everything else she touched was true.

Panel 30.4

The truth, shown to the reader and to no one in the room: the east span in the rain, charge housings down its spine glowing faintly with standby lights in the dark — alive, armed, patient — and far above them the detonator's home, in a masked man's camp, in a masked man's hand's reach.

The east span charges were live. Danny held the detonator. And his men would not pull back at dawn. The lie rode all the way toward the bridge — unless Rook spent his truth, or Sara burned her cover to stop it herself. Neither had happened. Yet.

Panel 30.5

The war room, last beat: Ian looking down at the diagram he trusts, the city leaning in around him, the café light burning in the window behind them all — the name, the net, the plan, the lie, arranged on one table like a hand of cards nobody's shown the reader twice.

IAN: "Good intel. We build on it."

The city had learned his name. Danny had learned it earlier — and had been writing it into his own ledger all along, in ink. The light stays on.
